In the lectures,
we took data that wasn't "tidy",
reshaped it,
summarized it,
and then used it to fit linear and logistic regressions.
In this homework,
you'll go through these steps yourself on new data.
In Part 1,
we'll tidy and summarize the Ebola case counts
from the 2014–2015 West Africa outbreak.
In Part 2,
you'll pick a clinical trial
and use a model to answer the question it asks.

Write your code in the empty code chunks
(the blocks that start with `{r}`),
and answer each question in full sentences underneath it.

## Part 1: Ebola case counts

`data/ebola.csv` has the number of Ebola cases and deaths in each country
from the 2014–2015 West Africa outbreak.
Caitlin Rivers compiled it from the WHO situation reports
([`cmrivers/ebola`](https://github.com/cmrivers/ebola),
`country_timeseries.csv`).

```{r}
ebola <- read_csv("data/ebola.csv")
ebola
```

### 1.1 Tidy the data

Notice that a column name like `Cases_Guinea` holds two variables,
the type of count (cases or deaths) and the country.
This is the same problem as the `who2` data from Lecture 1.
Make a new data frame, `ebola_tidy`,
with one row for each country in each report,
and a column each for the date, the country, the cases, and the deaths.
This will take a `pivot_longer()` that splits the column names,
and then a `pivot_wider()`.
The `Date` column is text,
so we'll also turn it into a real date with `mdy()`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Start from the `ebola` data frame.
Its columns are `Date`, `Day`, and one column for each count type and country,
such as `Cases_Guinea` and `Deaths_Liberia`.
Steps 1 and 2 are the same as the `who2` example in Lecture 1
([Split the header into three variables](https://chendaniely.github.io/MEDI-504A-2026W1-biostats/lecture-01/02-tidy-data.html#split-the-header-into-three-variables)).

1. Use
   [`pivot_longer()`](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/pivot_longer.html)
   on every column except `Date` and `Day`
   (`cols = -c(Date, Day)`),
   so each count gets its own row.
   Split each old column name at the underscore
   into two new columns, `type` and `country`,
   with `names_to = c("type", "country")` and `names_sep = "_"`.
   Put the numbers in a column called `count` (`values_to = "count"`),
   and drop the rows where the count is missing (`values_drop_na = TRUE`).
2. Use
   [`pivot_wider()`](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/pivot_wider.html)
   to turn the `type` column back into two columns,
   `Cases` and `Deaths`, with their values from `count`.
3. Use
   [`mutate()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate.html)
   and [`mdy()`](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/reference/ymd.html)
   to change `Date` from text into a date.
   `mdy()` reads dates written month/day/year, like `1/5/2015`.
   It comes from the lubridate package, which loads with the tidyverse
   (see [`mdy()`: dates from text](https://chendaniely.github.io/MEDI-504A-2026W1-biostats/lecture-02/06-extra-functions.html#mdy-dates-from-text)
   in Lecture 2's Extra functions slides).
4. Save the result as `ebola_tidy`,
   and put `ebola_tidy` on the last line of the chunk so it prints.

When it works,
the first line of the printed output says `# A tibble: 375 × 5`,
the columns are `Date`, `Day`, `country`, `Cases`, and `Deaths`,
and you'll see `<date>` under `Date`.
:::

### 1.2 Summarize by country

Now that our data is tidy,
let's summarize it by country.

The counts are **cumulative**.
Each report gives the total number of cases so far,
not the new cases since the last report.

Make a table with one row for each country.
It should have the date of the country's first and last report,
its number of cases and deaths,
and its case fatality ratio (the deaths divided by the cases).
Sort the table from the most cases to the fewest.

A few counts go down from one report to the next,
because a later report corrected an earlier one.
That means you can use either the last report or the largest count,
as long as you say which one you used.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Start from `ebola_tidy`.
Lecture 2's Extra functions slide
[`min()`, `max()`, and `desc()`](https://chendaniely.github.io/MEDI-504A-2026W1-biostats/lecture-02/06-extra-functions.html#min-max-and-desc)
does the same steps on the penguins.

1. Use
   [`group_by(country)`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/group_by.html)
   so the summary is calculated for each country.
2. Use
   [`summarize()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/summarise.html)
   to make these columns:
   - `first_report`, the earliest `Date`,
     with [`min()`](https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/base/html/Extremes.html)
   - `last_report`, the latest `Date`, with `max()`
   - `cases`, the largest value of `Cases`, with `max(Cases, na.rm = TRUE)`
   - `deaths`, the largest value of `Deaths`, with `max(Deaths, na.rm = TRUE)`

   `min()` gives the smallest value and `max()` the largest.
   For dates, the smallest is the earliest.
   `na.rm = TRUE` tells them to skip over missing values.
3. Use
   [`mutate()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate.html)
   to add `cfr`, the case fatality ratio, as `deaths / cases`.
4. Use
   [`arrange()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/arrange.html)
   with [`desc(cases)`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/desc.html)
   to sort from the most cases to the fewest.
   `desc()` stands for descending, so the largest comes first.
5. Save the result as `ebola_summary`,
   and put `ebola_summary` on the last line of the chunk so it prints.

This uses the largest count,
so write "I used the largest count" in your answer below.

When it works,
the first line of the printed output says `# A tibble: 8 × 6`,
and the first row is `SierraLeone`, with `10030` cases.
:::

## Part 2: A model

For Part 2,
pick one of these three clinical trials.
Each one comes with a question for you to answer with a model.
Before you start,
read the trial's page on the medicaldata website
to see what each variable means and how it's coded.

- [`laryngoscope`](https://higgi13425.github.io/medicaldata/reference/laryngoscope.html):
  99 adults with obesity who needed a breathing tube for elective surgery
  were randomized to a standard Macintosh laryngoscope
  or a Pentax AWS video laryngoscope.
  Does the video laryngoscope change how long intubation takes?
- [`indo_rct`](https://higgi13425.github.io/medicaldata/reference/indo_rct.html):
  602 patients at high risk of pancreatitis after ERCP
  were randomized to rectal indomethacin or a placebo.
  Does indomethacin prevent pancreatitis after ERCP?
- [`strep_tb`](https://higgi13425.github.io/medicaldata/reference/strep_tb.html):
  in the 1948 Medical Research Council trial,
  107 patients with pulmonary tuberculosis
  were randomized to streptomycin with bed rest or to bed rest alone.
  Did streptomycin make patients more likely to improve
  on their chest X-ray at 6 months?

Which trial did you pick?

### 2.1 Clean the variables you need

Like a lot of the data we get,
these trials store some of their categories as codes.
Recode the outcome, the treatment,
and any other variables you plan to use.
Numbers that stand for categories, like `0` and `1`,
should become factors with readable labels,
and labels like `1_yes` or `2_male` should become `yes` and `male`.
Then check the **reference level** of each factor,
the level that the other levels get compared to.
For the treatment,
the reference level should be the control group.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

A **factor** is how R stores a categorical variable.
Recode your variables the same way as the lab's
[Coded variables exercise](https://chendaniely.github.io/MEDI-504A-2026W1-biostats/lecture-02/02-clean-and-tidy.html#exercise-2-coded-variables).
Use [`mutate()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate.html)
with [`factor(column, levels = ..., labels = ...)`](https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/base/html/factor.html)
to turn coded values into categories with readable names.
The first level you list becomes the reference level,
so list the control group first.
Then use [`select()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/select.html)
to keep only the columns you need,
and [`drop_na()`](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/drop_na.html)
to drop the rows with missing values in them.
Save the result as `trial`.

Here's what to recode in each trial (its page has the details):

- `laryngoscope`:
  `Randomization` is 0 = Macintosh, 1 = video laryngoscope,
  and `gender` is 0 = female, 1 = male.
  The intubation time is `total_intubation_time`, in seconds.
  `age` and `BMI` are already numbers.
- `indo_rct`:
  `outcome` is `0_no` or `1_yes` (pancreatitis after ERCP),
  `rx` is `0_placebo` or `1_indomethacin`,
  and `gender` is `1_female` or `2_male`.
  `age` and `risk` (a risk score) are already numbers.
- `strep_tb`:
  `improved` is `TRUE` or `FALSE`,
  so make it a factor with `FALSE` as `no` and `TRUE` as `yes`.
  `arm` lists `Streptomycin` first,
  so use [`fct_relevel(arm, "Control")`](https://forcats.tidyverse.org/reference/fct_relevel.html)
  to make `Control` the reference level
  (see Lecture 2's Extra functions slide
  [`fct_relevel()` and `fct_collapse()`](https://chendaniely.github.io/MEDI-504A-2026W1-biostats/lecture-02/06-extra-functions.html#fct_relevel-and-fct_collapse)).
  `baseline_condition` is `1_Good`, `2_Fair`, or `3_Poor`.
  `gender` and `baseline_cavitation` are already readable.

End the chunk with `head(trial)`, so it prints the first 6 rows.
`trial` is a base R data frame, like the dataset it came from,
so printing `trial` itself would print every row.

To check your work,
run [`count()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/count.html)
on each column you recoded, for example `count(trial, arm)`.
You should see readable labels, not numbers or codes,
with the control group listed first.
:::

### 2.3 Fit a model

Should your outcome get a linear or a logistic regression?
Say why in one sentence,
based on what your plot in 2.2 shows.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

A linear regression models the average of an outcome
that's a number on a continuous scale, like a weight or a time.
A logistic regression models the odds of one of two outcomes,
like yes or no.
We fit one of each in Lecture 2's
Linear regression and Logistic regression sections.
Which kind of plot did you need in 2.2?
:::

*Your answer here.*

Now fit the model with the treatment and at least one other variable,
and show the estimates with their confidence intervals using `tidy()`.
For a logistic regression,
use `exponentiate = TRUE` to get odds ratios.
If an estimate or its confidence interval comes out enormous,
count that variable against the outcome to see why.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

A model formula puts the outcome on the left of the `~`
and the explanatory variables on the right, joined by `+`,
for example `outcome ~ treatment + age`.
Use your own column names in place of `outcome` and `treatment`.

1. Fit the model the same way we did in the lab.
   Start with [`linear_reg()`](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/reference/linear_reg.html)
   or [`logistic_reg()`](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/reference/logistic_reg.html),
   then use `|>` to pass it to [`fit()`](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/reference/fit.html)
   with your formula and `data = trial`,
   like `linear_reg() |> fit(outcome ~ treatment + age, data = trial)`.
   Save the result as `trial_fit`.
2. Use `tidy(trial_fit, conf.int = TRUE)` to see the estimates
   with their 95% confidence intervals
   (see `tidy()` for a
   [linear](https://broom.tidymodels.org/reference/tidy.lm.html)
   or a [logistic](https://broom.tidymodels.org/reference/tidy.glm.html) model).
   For a logistic regression, add `exponentiate = TRUE`
   to turn the estimates into odds ratios.

If an estimate is huge (with an `e+` in it, like `4.6e+07`)
or a confidence limit is `NA`,
run `count(trial, that_variable, outcome)`
and look for a group where every patient had the same outcome.
The model can't estimate an effect for that group,
so leave the variable out,
or combine its levels with
[`fct_collapse()`](https://forcats.tidyverse.org/reference/fct_collapse.html)
(see Lecture 2's Extra functions slide
[`fct_relevel()` and `fct_collapse()`](https://chendaniely.github.io/MEDI-504A-2026W1-biostats/lecture-02/06-extra-functions.html#fct_relevel-and-fct_collapse)).

Make the `tidy()` line the last line of the chunk,
so its table prints.

### 2.4 What does the model say?

Interpret at least two variables from your model in full sentences.
For each one,
say how big the effect is and in which direction,
in the outcome's units (or as an odds ratio),
along with its confidence interval.
Then use your model to answer the trial's question.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Each row of your `tidy()` output after the intercept is one variable.
For a category,
the estimate compares that group with the reference level
(the control group, for the treatment).
For a number,
the estimate is the change for every 1 unit increase,
such as one more year of age.
As in Lecture 1,
each estimate is the change for one variable
when the other variables stay the same
(you'll also see this written as "all else equal").

You can fill in a sentence like one of these:

- Linear regression, for a category:
  "When the other variables stay the same,
  patients who [group] had an average [outcome]
  [estimate] [units] [higher or lower] than patients who [reference group]
  (95% CI: [conf.low] to [conf.high])."
- Linear regression, for a number:
  "When the other variables stay the same,
  every 1 [unit] increase in [variable] went with an average [outcome]
  [estimate] [units] [higher or lower]
  (95% CI: [conf.low] to [conf.high])."
- Logistic regression, for a category:
  "When the other variables stay the same,
  patients who [group] had [estimate] times the odds of [outcome]
  of patients who [reference group]
  (odds ratio [estimate], 95% CI: [conf.low] to [conf.high])."
- Logistic regression, for a number:
  "When the other variables stay the same,
  the odds of [outcome] were multiplied by [estimate]
  for every 1 [unit] increase in [variable]
  (95% CI: [conf.low] to [conf.high])."

An odds ratio below 1 means lower odds,
and above 1 means higher odds.
If a confidence interval includes 0 (for a linear regression)
or 1 (for a logistic regression),
the data don't show a clear effect for that variable.
Finish by answering the trial's question with yes or no,
and in which direction.
:::

*Your answer here.*
